Rather than adding another round of advocacy to the disclosure debate, Anderson's contribution is empirical: the article draws on two federal courts that have actually mandated disclosure of third-party funding in cases before them, the U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey, and, under its chief judge, the U.S. District Court for the District of Delaware, to look behind what the article calls the industry's opaque curtain and establish what funded litigation actually looks like where the data exists, rather than relying on the anecdote and advocacy that has otherwise dominated the debate.

The finding matters for how to weigh the rest of this debate: much of the fight over TPLF disclosure, including the pending federal bills covered elsewhere in this library, has been argued in the abstract, by parties with an obvious stake in the outcome. Two courts already generating real disclosure data offer a preview of what broader, state or federal, disclosure requirements might actually reveal, and a way to test the competing claims made about litigation funding's effects against something other than each side's priors.
sources: Demystifying Third-Party Litigation Funding, George Washington Law Review
Third-Party Litigation Funding, Utah Law Review (companion piece)

articles.title: Preventive Transparency: A Narrower Path to Funding Disclosure
articles.teaser: A 2025 law review proposal grounds disclosure not in new legislation, but in rules already on the books.
body: Years of attempts to comprehensively regulate third-party litigation funding at the federal level have gone nowhere, stuck in the same disclosure-versus-confidentiality stalemate covered elsewhere in this library. In a 2025 Northwestern University Law Review article, “Preventive Transparency in Third-Party Litigation Funding,” law professor Seth Katsuya Endo proposes a narrower way through: rather than arguing for what disclosure policy should look like from first principles, the article asks what current law, federal civil procedure and professional-responsibility rules already on the books, requires, and works out the implications for funding transparency from there.

The resulting proposal is deliberately modest. Grounding the analysis in the federal judicial disqualification statute and nationally uniform professional-conduct rules, Endo argues litigants should, at minimum, be required to disclose, in camera, to the judge, not necessarily to opposing counsel or the public, both the existence of any third-party funding agreement and any provision giving the funder control over the litigation. That is a meaningfully narrower ask than the public, filed-of-record disclosure sought by the pending federal bills covered elsewhere in this library: it protects the confidentiality funders and claimants generally want, while still giving a judge the visibility needed to police the specific conflict-of-interest and independence concerns those existing ethics rules already exist to catch.

The timing is notable. The article was published as the federal judiciary's own Advisory Committee on Civil Rules agreed, for the first time, to take up litigation funding disclosure as a potential subject for a new procedural rule, meaning a doctrinally modest proposal like this one, built from rules already in force rather than new legislation, may be a more realistic near-term path to some form of federal disclosure than the more sweeping bills currently stalled in Congress.
sources: Preventive Transparency in Third-Party Litigation Funding, Northwestern University Law Review
S.3826, Litigation Funding Transparency Act of 2026, Congress.gov

articles.title: How Insurers See It: Social Inflation and the Cost Debate
articles.teaser: The industry's own case against litigation funding, and why it's more contested than the numbers alone suggest.
body: Everything covered elsewhere in this library largely takes the perspective of claimants, funders, and the lawyers who work with both. The insurance industry sees the same market very differently, as a meaningful driver of what it calls “social inflation”: liability claims costs rising faster than wages, medical costs, or general prices can explain. Swiss Re Institute's sigma 4/2024 report, the first to formally isolate a “Social Inflation Index” from ordinary economic inflation, found the U.S. figure averaged 5.4% annually from 2017 to 2022 and peaked near 7% in 2023, a trend the Institute says shows no sign of abating. So-called “nuclear verdicts” (jury awards of $10 million or more) rose 52% in 2024 to a record 135 cases, and “thermonuclear” verdicts above $100 million rose even faster, with five individual verdicts exceeding $1 billion that year alone.

Insurers name third-party litigation funding specifically as one accelerant among several. The mechanism they describe is straightforward: by covering upfront costs and absorbing the downside risk of a loss, funding lets plaintiffs reject early settlement offers and hold out for trial, where the largest verdicts are possible, extending case durations and pushing the overall distribution of outcomes toward higher-value results. That framing has already produced real policy: Georgia's 2025 tort reform, for instance, now requires litigation funders to register with the state's Department of Banking and Finance and can hold them jointly and severally liable for frivolous litigation, and several other states enacted comparable funder-specific provisions the same year.

It's worth stating plainly that this is an interested party's account, not a neutral one, in exactly the way that funder-commissioned research arguing funding improves case screening (covered elsewhere in this library) is also an interested party's account. The insurance industry has a direct financial stake in attributing rising claims costs to an external cause rather than to its own pricing and underwriting choices, and researchers outside the industry point to shifting juror demographics, declining institutional trust, and plaintiff-side trial strategy as at least equally significant drivers of the same verdict data. What isn't contested is that this is now a live, well-funded regulatory fight, not a settled question, and litigation funding has become a central, named target in it.
sources: sigma 4/2024: Social Inflation, Litigation Costs Drive Claims Inflation, Swiss Re Institute

articles.title: Why Litigation Funding Works Like Venture Capital, Not a Loan
articles.teaser: The academic reframe that explains why funding agreements look the way they do, priced like a startup raising a round, not underwritten like a loan.
body: The first instinct most claimants bring to a funding conversation is a lending frame: what is the rate, when is it due, what happens if I cannot pay. That frame is wrong, and understanding why changes how you should negotiate. In her 2012 William & Mary Law Review article "The Litigation Finance Contract," Maya Steinitz argued that earlier scholarship had reached for the wrong analogy when it compared funding to a contingency fee arrangement. The better comparison, she argued, is venture capital, because both relationships share the same three structural features: extreme uncertainty about the eventual outcome, a severe information gap between the party who knows the underlying facts and the party supplying the money, and high agency costs once capital is committed and incentives can drift apart.

That reframe is not academic decoration. It explains concrete features of a real funding agreement that a lending frame cannot. Funding is non-recourse, like an equity check and unlike a loan, because the funder is buying a contingent stake in an outcome rather than lending against a borrower's general ability to repay. Funders ask for detailed information rights and regular case updates for the same reason a venture investor asks for board reporting, not because they distrust the claimant, but because the information asymmetry that made the deal necessary in the first place does not close on the day the check is signed. The empirical record backs the analogy: a 2003 study of real venture financings by Steven Kaplan and Per Strömberg of the University of Chicago Booth School of Business found that actual VC contracts separately allocate cash flow rights, board rights, voting rights, and liquidation rights, with roughly 15 percent of financings providing only partial funding at signing, additional capital contingent on the company hitting subsequent milestones. Litigation funders have adapted essentially that same toolkit to claims.

The practical implication for a claimant or a lawyer evaluating a term sheet is to stop asking what the interest rate is and start asking the questions a founder asks before taking a term sheet: what does the investor get in exchange for the risk they are absorbing, what happens if more capital is needed later on different terms, and what information is owed along the way. A funding agreement is a form of equity financing for a lawsuit, and negotiating it like a debt instrument means missing most of what is actually being asked.
sources: The Litigation Finance Contract, William & Mary Law Review
Financial Contracting Theory Meets the Real World, Kaplan & Strömberg, SSRN

articles.title: Staged Funding and Why Your Second Check Is Priced Differently
articles.teaser: Nobody can price a lawsuit accurately at the outset. That is why funders release capital in tranches, and why the pricing logic changes with each one.
body: A claim cannot be priced accurately the day a funding agreement is signed, because the information that would make it possible to price accurately, how a key witness holds up under deposition, how a court rules on a dispositive motion, what an expert's damages number actually looks like once tested, does not exist yet. Maya Steinitz confronted this problem directly in her 2013 Vanderbilt Law Review article "How Much Is That Lawsuit in the Window? Pricing Legal Claims," and her answer is the reason almost every real funding agreement releases capital in tranches tied to specific case milestones such as surviving a motion to dismiss, completing key depositions, or obtaining an expert report.

Steinitz's framing borrows a tool from corporate finance: real options theory. Each tranche decision is best understood as a call option, the right but not the obligation to fund the next stage of the case once some of the uncertainty present at signing has resolved. As the case moves forward and genuinely new information arrives, both sides revise their view of what the claim is worth, and the price attached to the next tranche reflects that updated view rather than the terms struck at the very beginning. This is why litigation finance is sometimes described as a series of compound options rather than a single investment decision.

The practical lesson for a claimant is to read a staged agreement for what it actually says happens at each decision point, not to assume the deal signed on day one governs the whole case. Ask specifically what triggers a tranche release, what information the funder is entitled to before deciding whether to fund the next stage, and what happens contractually, not just informally, if the funder declines to advance further capital after an adverse ruling. A funder's decision not to fund a later tranche is very often a contractually anticipated outcome built into the structure from the start, not a sign of bad faith.
sources: How Much Is That Lawsuit in the Window? Pricing Legal Claims, Vanderbilt Law Review

articles.title: What's Actually In a Funding Agreement
articles.teaser: Funding contracts are not standardized, and most claimants see their first one with no benchmark for what is normal. Here is the benchmark, provision by provision.
body: Litigation finance contracts are not standardized the way a residential mortgage or a car loan is. Terms vary widely across funders, claim types, and jurisdictions, and most claimants encounter their first funding agreement with no real benchmark for what is customary versus unusual. In 2014, Maya Steinitz and Abigail C. Field tried to close that gap directly, publishing "A Model Litigation Finance Contract" in the Iowa Law Review after developing it through an open research process at litigationfinancecontract.com, where each draft provision was posted for public comment and revised in response before the final version went to print.

The model contract is organized around a handful of provision categories worth knowing before reading a real one. The funding mechanics set out the amount committed, whether it is released as a single payment or in tranches tied to case milestones, and the return waterfall, typically a return of capital plus the greater of a fixed multiple or a percentage of recovery. The control provisions are usually the most heavily negotiated: well-drafted agreements reserve litigation strategy, settlement authority, and privileged communications to the claimant and counsel, while giving the funder information rights and case updates, often with a consultation right on major decisions short of an actual veto. Termination and default provisions specify what happens if the claimant settles without consent or the funder stops advancing capital partway through. Confidentiality and assignment provisions govern who else may see the agreement and whether the funder's interest can be sold or syndicated without the claimant's consent.

None of this substitutes for independent counsel reviewing a specific agreement before signing. But knowing the standard shape of a funding contract in advance is the difference between negotiating from a position of information and negotiating blind.
sources: A Model Litigation Finance Contract, Iowa Law Review

articles.title: Who Controls a Funded Case?
articles.teaser: Once money is attached to a claim, the claimant is no longer the only party with an interest in how it is litigated. The scholarship names this problem and its worst-case failure mode.
body: Rule 5.4(c) and its state analogues formally bar a funder from directing litigation strategy, but the rule does not resolve the underlying governance problem it was written to contain. In her 2015 Notre Dame Law Review article "Incorporating Legal Claims," Maya Steinitz argued that nearly every hard problem litigation finance produces is a version of one classic corporate governance issue: the separation of ownership from control. Once a funder holds an economic stake in an outcome it does not direct, the claimant's formal authority over the case and the funder's financial interest in how it resolves can quietly pull apart, even when every individual actor is behaving in good faith.

Steinitz's more recent work sharpens the worst-case version of that drift. Her paper "Zombie Litigation: Claim Aggregation, Litigant Autonomy, and Funders' Intermeddling," forthcoming in the Cornell Law Review, coins the term to describe a governance failure in which real control over a claim migrates away from the claimant toward funders and attorneys acting less like advisors and more like asset managers, with the nominal plaintiff technically still in charge but functionally along for the ride. She situates the risk within the growth of aggregate and portfolio funding, structures where a single funder holds stakes across many claims at once.

The practical guardrail for a claimant is to read a funding agreement specifically for what it reserves to the claimant, settlement approval authority, control over litigation strategy, and the ability to change counsel, rather than assuming those rights survive by default. It is also worth asking directly how the party helping evaluate a claim is compensated. A flat fee agreed in advance, paid regardless of whether funding is ultimately offered or accepted, keeps that party's incentives aligned with getting the analysis right rather than steering toward any particular funder, which is precisely the kind of structural answer this literature calls for.
sources: Incorporating Legal Claims, Notre Dame Law Review

articles.title: Should Funding Agreements Be Disclosed?
articles.teaser: Whether your funding agreement is discoverable is a live question in most jurisdictions. The academic framework courts and legislatures are actually arguing over.
body: The domestic fight over disclosure has its own academic anchor, separate from the European regulatory push covered elsewhere in this library. In her 2019 U.C. Davis Law Review article "Follow the Money? A Proposed Approach for Disclosure of Litigation Finance Agreements," Maya Steinitz argued that the search for one bright-line disclosure rule, always require it or never require it, is the wrong project, because funding scenarios vary too widely in stakes, sophistication of the parties, and risk of genuine conflict for a single rule to fit all of them well. Her proposal instead is a balancing test, applied case by case.

That framework maps onto a currently unsettled legal landscape. A handful of states have passed specific litigation-funding disclosure statutes requiring funding agreements to be disclosed in certain circumstances. Federal courts remain split on whether a funding agreement is automatically discoverable or protected as attorney work product, and proposed federal legislation addressing disclosure has been introduced in Congress without yet becoming law. Steinitz's September 2023 written testimony before the U.S. House Committee on Oversight and Accountability, given during a hearing specifically on third-party litigation funding transparency, is a compact and freely available statement of where federal attention is currently pointed.

The practical implication is to assume a funding agreement could become discoverable in a given jurisdiction, even if current law suggests otherwise, because that law is actively being litigated and legislated. That argues for keeping privileged litigation strategy discussions out of the funding agreement itself and in genuinely separate, properly protected communications with counsel.
sources: Follow the Money? A Proposed Approach for Disclosure of Litigation Finance Agreements, U.C. Davis Law Review
Written Testimony of Maya Steinitz, U.S. House Committee on Oversight

articles.title: What Is a Law Firm MSO?
articles.teaser: The two-company structure letting outside capital buy the business side of law firms: what the MSO owns, what must stay with the lawyers, and where the legal line actually sits.
body: Rule 5.4 and its state analogues bar nonlawyers from owning law firms or sharing in legal fees, which is why private equity, so visible in medicine, dentistry, and accounting, was long absent from law. The management services organization, or MSO, is the structure through which that changed. The firm is split into two companies. One, owned only by licensed lawyers, keeps the legal practice: the clients, the files, the fee agreements, and the professional judgment. The other, the MSO, acquires substantially everything else, the staff, the technology, the billing and collections operation, the leases, the marketing, and outside investors own that company freely. A master services agreement connects the two: the MSO runs the business side for a recurring fee, and the law firm practices law. The lawyers get capital and, for retiring founders, an exit that law firm economics never otherwise offered. The investors get recurring services revenue from one of the largest and least consolidated professional sectors in the economy.

The scale is no longer hypothetical. One law firm's legal services transactions team, the most visible in this niche, reported closing seven MSO deals in 2025 and roughly twenty across twenty states by mid-2026, with around one hundred more in its pipeline, spanning AmLaw 100 practice groups, AI-native boutiques, estate planning shops, and personal injury firms. What makes the structure legal comes down mostly to one clause: the fee. Texas Ethics Opinion 706, the first modern opinion to address MSOs directly, held that an MSO may not be paid a percentage of firm revenue, because that is fee-splitting with a nonlawyer however labeled, while confirming that a properly structured MSO charging fair-market fixed fees is permissible. The MSO also must not set legal fees, direct case strategy, decide settlements, or control lawyer hiring, because those powers are the practice of law and cannot be sold.

For anyone connected to litigation finance, three things matter. An MSO is not funding: the money buys the firm's business assets, not a stake in claim outcomes. The two markets are converging anyway, because funders increasingly lend at the firm level and MSO investors increasingly sit next to contingency fee streams, which is why regulators have begun addressing both in the same statutes. And the legal ground is moving fast: between February 2025 and August 2026, Texas, California, Colorado, and Illinois each drew lines around the model, all of them striking at revenue-linked compensation rather than at the structure itself.
sources: Private Equity MSO Deal Lawyers, LawFuel

articles.title: The State Backlash: Four Jurisdictions Draw the MSO Line
articles.teaser: In eighteen months, Texas, California, Colorado, and Illinois each drew lines around outside capital in law firms. Every one struck the same feature, and it was not the MSO itself.
body: The sequence ran fast. In February 2025, Texas Ethics Opinion 706 held that a lawyer may not pay a services company a percentage of firm revenue, that is fee-splitting with a nonlawyer however dressed, while confirming the MSO structure itself is permissible on fixed, fair-market fees. In October 2025, California enacted AB 931, barring its lawyers from sharing fees with out-of-state alternative business structures for four years, aimed at Arizona's ABS program, with statutory damages of $10,000 per violation. In June 2026, Colorado signed HB26-1421, lifting the fee-sharing prohibition into statute for three years, effectively barring ABS models, restricting MSO fees, and creating a private right of action so clients themselves can sue. And on August 7, 2026, Illinois approved Public Act 104-0801, targeting MSOs owned or controlled by private equity and hedge funds specifically, barring fees based directly or indirectly on the firm's fees, revenues, or profits, and prohibiting such owners from interfering with professional judgment.

Look at the four together and a pattern emerges that most commentary has missed: not one of them prohibits the MSO. Every one strikes the same feature, compensation linked to legal revenue. California even wrote the compliant design into statute as an express exemption: contracts that charge a flat fee, pay nothing for referrals or lead generation, and do not scale with recovery are outside the ban entirely. Colorado permits a funder to lend against identified case proceeds at a capped multiple while banning any share of firm fees, revenues, or profits. Four regulators, working separately across eighteen months, converged on one principle: capital may be paid for services at fixed prices, and capital may buy claims, but capital may not meter its return on the practice of law. Two of the statutes also sunset, California's after four years and Colorado's after three, so the states are running term-limited experiments while Arizona runs the opposite one.

Three practical readings. For law firm owners, the fee clause is the whole ballgame: a fixed, fair-market service fee survives everywhere these rules have reached. For funders, Colorado's safe harbor is the sentence to memorize, because it makes deal structure outcome-determinative: a portfolio facility collateralized by identified cases with a capped return sits inside the harbor, while anything resembling revenue participation sits outside it, in a state where clients now hold a private right of action. And Colorado's private enforcement means the first judicial interpretations of these boundaries will likely come from litigation rather than bar proceedings.

articles.title: The Third Rung: How Outside Capital Climbed from the Claim to the Firm
articles.teaser: Litigation finance and the law firm MSO wave are one phenomenon at different altitudes. The same three questions follow the money at every level, and AI is why the third level is happening now.
body: Outside capital has entered legal practice three times, at three altitudes, and each arrival was treated as a novel controversy when it was really the same event repeating. The first rung was the claim: non-recourse capital invested in a single dispute, which had to fight past centuries of champerty doctrine to exist. The second rung was the portfolio and the firm's balance sheet: funders lending against baskets of cases and contingency fee inventories. The third rung, arriving now through the management services organization, is the firm itself, with investors buying everything a law firm is except the part that is legally a law firm. The same three questions follow the money at every rung: who controls legal judgment once someone else's capital depends on it, who may share in the fees that judgment produces, and what happens when the investor's interest and the client's interest pull apart. Illinois's new statute barring MSO owners from interfering with professional judgment is Rule 5.4(c) restated for a new buyer, and its ban on revenue-based fees is fee-splitting doctrine restated for a new contract.

Maya Steinitz saw this coming before the deal flow arrived. Her 2022 article The Partnership Mystique argued that the financial products then entering the legal market were functionally equivalent to owning law firms and would raise every governance problem that direct nonlawyer ownership raises. The MSO wave has spent 2025 and 2026 proving her right. What her article could not yet name was the accelerant: artificial intelligence collapsed the achievable cost of the legal back office. Intake, billing, collections, document handling, and much of marketing can now run at a fraction of historical cost, but most small and mid-sized firms still carry the historical cost structure. An MSO purchase is, at bottom, an arbitrage on that spread: buy the back office at a price reflecting how it has always been run, operate it at what it now costs to run, and keep the difference.

Which makes the regulatory response coherent. Texas's Opinion 706, California's AB 931, Colorado's HB26-1421, and Illinois's Public Act 104-0801 differ in mechanism but converge on a single line: none prohibits the structure, and all prohibit metering capital's return on legal revenue. Notice what that line distinguishes. It permits the cost-side MSO, one that earns a fixed fair-market fee and profits by running the back office more efficiently than the fee assumes, and it forbids the revenue-side MSO, one that profits by taking a growing slice of what the lawyers bill. The two look similar on a term sheet and are opposites in incentive: a cost-side operator gets rich by making the firm cheaper to run, while a revenue-side operator gets rich the way a contingent owner would, by pushing the practice to bill more, which is precisely what the fee-splitting rule has existed for a century to prevent. The AI arbitrage does not need the forbidden structure; its economics live entirely on the cost side, so the version of this wave that survives regulation and the version that makes economic sense are the same version.

The principle will be familiar to readers of this Institute, because the field keeps arriving at it from every direction. The litigation finance literature concluded that an advisor compensated by flat fee, paid regardless of outcome, is structurally aligned with getting the analysis right. The funding industry's own defense rests on buying an interest in a claim rather than a share of the lawyer's fee. And now four regulators, examining capital at the level of the firm, have drawn the identical boundary: capital may be paid for services at a fixed price, and capital may buy claims, but capital may not meter itself on the practice of law. That is the rule of the whole ladder, stated once per rung. For claimants the simple form is this: the capital structure behind your law firm now shapes who profits from your case, and the question worth asking is never whether outside money is present, but how it gets paid.
sources: Primary Sources: Capital at the level of the firm
Private Equity and Law Firm MSOs: The 2026 Reckoning, LawFuel
The Partnership Mystique, William & Mary Law Review (via our Foundational Scholarship page)

articles.title: When the Settlement Is Not the Money: Liens, Fees, and the Interpleader
articles.teaser: A settlement figure is the top of a waterfall. The fee, the costs, and every lien come out before the claimant, and an interpleader can freeze what is left. What each deduction is, which ones are negotiable, and the questions that sometimes bring money back.
body: A settlement figure is the top of a waterfall, not the amount that reaches the claimant. Before anything is paid out, the contingency fee comes off, then the costs the lawyer advanced during the case, then every lien that attaches to the recovery: hospitals and treating providers who were never paid, the health insurer or Medicare or Medicaid that paid them, sometimes a workers' compensation carrier or a child support agency. What is left belongs to the client. The arithmetic can be brutal. A $150,000 settlement with a 40 percent fee loses $60,000 at the first step, perhaps $8,000 in costs at the second, and if $70,000 in medical liens follows, the claimant nets $12,000. Nothing has gone wrong in the legal sense; this is simply how the money flows. But the number the claimant was told and the number the claimant receives can differ by an order of magnitude, and most people learn this only when the disbursement statement arrives.

Liens are the largest deduction and the least fixed. Every major kind carries its own reduction rule, and whether counsel invoked it is the first question a claimant should ask. Medicare's claim is a federal statutory right, but the regulation that governs it, 42 CFR 411.37, requires Medicare to reduce its recovery by its proportional share of the attorney's fees and costs it took to produce the settlement; Medicare pays its share of the lawyer, in other words. Medicaid is constrained by the Supreme Court's decisions in Arkansas Department of Health and Human Services v. Ahlborn (2006) and Wos v. E.M.A. (2013): a state may recover only from the portion of a settlement attributable to medical expenses, not from the part that compensates pain, lost wages, or anything else, so a settlement that is a fraction of the claim's full value supports a proportional cut to the lien. Private health plans depend on how they are organized. A self-funded employer plan governed by ERISA can enforce whatever its plan document says, and after U.S. Airways v. McCutchen (2013) that language controls; but where the plan is silent, the common fund doctrine applies and the plan shares the fee, and after Montanile (2016) the plan must be able to trace its claim to funds still in the claimant's hands. State-regulated insurers are usually subject to state made-whole and anti-subrogation rules that cut the other way. Hospital liens are creatures of state statute and are often capped; California's Hospital Lien Act limits a hospital to half of what remains after the attorney's fee and prior liens are paid. None of this happens automatically. It happens because someone asks.

The fee is a contract, and it is regulated. A third before suit and 40 percent after filing is common, but the retainer agreement controls, several states cap personal injury fees or impose sliding scales that fall as the recovery rises, and medical malpractice fees are capped by statute in California and elsewhere. Two details in the retainer decide more than the headline rate: whether the percentage is taken from the gross settlement or from the amount left after costs, and whether costs are charged before or after the fee is computed. A claimant who believes the fee was miscalculated, or that a lien should have been negotiated harder, has a formal remedy that costs nothing: every state bar runs a fee dispute or fee arbitration program, and in many states the lawyer must participate if the client elects it. A second opinion from an unaffiliated lawyer, through the bar's referral service, is the sensible first step before invoking it.

The interpleader is what happens when the people claiming the money cannot agree on how to split it. Whoever is holding the funds, usually the defendant's insurer or the claimant's own lawyer holding them in trust, deposits the money with the court and asks the court to decide who gets what. Federal law provides for it in 28 U.S.C. 1335 and Rule 22 of the civil rules, and every state has an equivalent. It protects the holder from paying twice; for the claimant it means the money is frozen until a judge rules on priority, which can take months. One rule matters here more than any other. Under Rule 1.15 of the rules of professional conduct, a lawyer holding funds that others claim must keep the disputed portion in trust, but must promptly pay out any portion that is not in dispute. If the liens and the fee together claim $118,000 of a $150,000 settlement, the remaining $32,000 is not in dispute, and the claimant is entitled to ask for it now rather than wait for the interpleader to resolve the rest.

Litigation finance does not fit this situation, and it is better to say so plainly than to send someone searching. Commercial funders invest in unresolved claims in exchange for a share of a future recovery; a settled case with a fixed pot is not an investment, it is an accounting. Post-settlement advance companies do exist. They lend against a claimant's expected net share, at rates that compound monthly, and they will not lend against a share that may be zero or against a fund an interpleader has frozen. For a claimant whose net is small and uncertain, the honest answer is that there is no bridge product, and the money to be found is in the deductions themselves: a Medicare reduction not taken, a Medicaid lien not apportioned, a hospital lien above its statutory cap, a fee computed on the wrong base, an undisputed balance sitting in trust. Ask for the disbursement statement in writing, with every lien, its amount, and the reduction sought. Ask which reduction rule was applied to each. Ask what portion is undisputed. Then, if the answers are unsatisfying, the fee dispute program and a second opinion. None of this is legal advice; it is a map of where the money went and the questions that sometimes bring some of it back.
sources: 42 CFR 411.37, Amount of Medicare recovery when a primary payment is made as a result of a judgment or settlement (eCFR)
Arkansas Dept. of Health and Human Servs. v. Ahlborn, 547 U.S. 268 (2006)
Wos v. E.M.A., 568 U.S. 627 (2013), Cornell LII
U.S. Airways, Inc. v. McCutchen, 569 U.S. 88 (2013), Georgetown Law
California Civil Code section 3045.4, Hospital Lien Act (FindLaw)

articles.title: Delaware Superior Court Adopts a Limited Discovery Rule for Litigation Funding Agreements
articles.teaser: A new Delaware Superior Court rule lets opponents learn that litigation funding exists and who controls settlement, but keeps the agreement's terms and shared case information protected by default.
body: On September 30, 2026, the Delaware Superior Court amended its Civil Rule 26(b) to add a new subsection (b)(3) on litigation-funding agreements, according to a Reed Smith summary published October 5, 2026. In short, an opponent may learn that a funding arrangement exists and who is behind it, but not what the agreement says. This article explains what the rule covers, what it protects, and what it means for someone seeking funding for a case that could be filed in Delaware.

As Reed Smith describes it, the rule defines a litigation-funding agreement as one in which a non-attorney counterparty pays a party's litigation expenses and holds two things: a right to repayment that depends on the outcome of the case, and a right to control some aspect of the litigation, such as approving a settlement. On that description, the definition turns on control. An arrangement that gives a funder repayment rights but no control rights would not fit it, although the actual rule text should be checked before anyone relies on that reading.

The rule permits discovery of only four things: that the agreement exists, who the parties to it are, how it meets the definition, and any specified control rights. Reed Smith reports that the agreement's contents, the case information the funded party shared with the funder, and the work product of the funder's attorney or representative are protected.

There is a narrow exception. The court may order production of the portion of the agreement that grants control rights, such as settlement approval, if the requesting party shows cause. The agreement is also not admissible at trial. Reed Smith notes that the rule applies only in the Superior Court and that the Court of Chancery has not adopted a similar rule, so a funded party in Delaware needs to know which court it is in.

The rule arrives while the federal system is weighing the same question. On October 7, 2026, the International Legal Finance Association, the funders' trade group, filed Rules Suggestion 26-CV-42 with the federal Advisory Committee on Civil Rules ahead of its October 21 meeting. ILFA cites Delaware's Rule 26(b)(3) and a Western District of Louisiana standing order as models that bar production of funding agreements without a court order while allowing limited disclosure of control rights. ILFA says the proposal from Lawyers for Civil Justice and the U.S. Chamber Institute for Legal Reform would instead require automatic disclosure to opponents. These are an interested party's characterizations, not holdings of any court.

ILFA also argues that courts already refuse most requests for funding agreements. Its own dataset of more than 475 actions, it says, found that only 19 of 163 disclosure orders (12 percent) required production of an agreement, each on a case-specific ground. Those figures come from the trade association and have not been independently checked here. Disclosure advocates make a different argument, that opponents and courts need to see who controls a case. Delaware's rule sits between the two positions: it reveals the fact of funding and the control terms, and keeps the financial terms and the strategy private by default.

For someone seeking funding, the practical points are these. If the case is in Delaware Superior Court, expect the other side to be able to ask whether a funder exists and whether it has settlement approval or other control rights. Know exactly what control rights your agreement gives, because those are the terms a court can order produced. Keep in mind that the rule is days old and we found no decision applying it. Ask your own lawyer how it interacts with privilege and work-product protection for the materials you share with a funder, and whether the case is more likely to be filed in the Superior Court or in Chancery.
sources: Reed Smith Viewpoints, Delaware Superior Court Adopts Rule Permitting Limited Discovery of Litigation-Funding Agreements, October 5, 2026 (law firm summary; the court's order itself was not located)
International Legal Finance Association, Rules Suggestion 26-CV-42 to the Advisory Committee on Civil Rules, October 7, 2026 (trade association submission)

articles.title: When a Funder Withdraws Mid-Case: Three Australian Class Actions That Ended Without a Decision
articles.teaser: Three funded Australian class actions ended because the funder stopped paying. Here is what the Federal Court looked at, what happened to group members, and what to ask before you sign.
body: Funded cases are supposed to end with a verdict, a settlement, or a loss the funder absorbs. Three recent Australian class actions ended another way: the funder stopped paying and the case stopped with it. Two Federal Court of Australia judgments and one set of news reports show what a court looks at when that happens, what happens to the people in the group, and what anyone considering funding should ask before signing. These are three examples, not proof of a trend, and Australian class action procedure differs from American practice.

The most recent is Buttgieg v Macquarie Bank Limited [2026] FCA 1500. Justice Derrington gave the applicant leave to discontinue on 1 October 2026, and the reasons were published in amended form on 9 October. The court listed four problems. The applicant did not appear to fit the group definition, which exposed the case to a strike-out risk. She believed the group might hold no more than thirteen people, and fewer than seven after opt-outs. Many potential members may already have been repaid by the bank. And the funder had terminated its arrangement after judging the case too risky, with no alternative funding in sight.

On funding, the judgment is direct. The court said the absence of funding materially impeded continuing the case, and noted that the funder's decision may reflect doubts about the claims' prospects. That is a useful reminder that a funder's exit is itself information. It is not only a financing event.

The consequences for the group were mild because the case ended early. There was no order as to costs, and group members will not be liable for any costs. The court ordered no further notice to potential members, reasoning that the group was very small and unidentified, the case had limited publicity, and the bank had never been served. Limitation periods were suspended from the start of the case under section 33ZE(1) of the Federal Court of Australia Act, so the court found that discontinuance created no limitation problem, while noting some uncertainty in the authorities about when time starts running again.

A June 2026 decision shows the harder version. In Inger v State of Queensland [2026] FCA 792, Justice Hespe approved discontinuance of a class action challenging Queensland's additional foreign acquirer duty and land tax surcharge. After the High Court's decision in G Global 120E T2 Pty Ltd v Commissioner of State Revenue [2025] HCA 39, handed down on 15 October 2025, the funder (referred to in the notice as CASL) no longer considered the case commercially viable. The lead lawyer advised there was no reasonable prospect of another funder stepping in, and the court accepted evidence to that effect. The respondents agreed to no order as to costs, and earlier costs orders were vacated. This judgment is older than this article's usual window, but it shows the other side of the coin: here the court ordered that limitation periods for group members begin running again 30 days after the date by which the applicants must file their notice of discontinuance, and the notice told members to seek urgent legal advice.

The third example rests on news reports because the court's reasons were not located. ABC News reported on 8 October 2026 that two Queensland child safety class actions in the Federal Court were being discontinued after the funder, identified as Therium, decided in September 2025 it no longer wanted to fund them. It reported that Justice Dowling noted the lawyers had made significant attempts to find alternative funding, and that the parties had to prepare a notice to group members. National Indigenous Times reported on 16 October 2026 that the case had been formally discontinued, that group members are not barred from suing again and are not liable for costs, and that $350,000 of the State's legal costs was to be paid by the funder rather than the lead applicants. The two outlets name slightly different Therium entities, and the costs detail comes from a single report, so treat it as unconfirmed until the order is published.

What ties these together is the test the Federal Court applies: whether discontinuance would be unfair, unreasonable or adverse to group members' interests. That test protects people through notice, costs and limitation periods. It does not restore a lost claim or a lost year. The practical differences between the cases were stark: no notice and a suspended clock in one, a restarted clock and an urgent-advice warning in another, and in the third a group member quoted as unsure she has the strength to start again.

For someone seeking or evaluating funding, the lesson is to read the exit terms as carefully as the price. Ask your lawyer whether the funding agreement lets the funder stop, on what grounds, and at what milestones. Ask who pays adverse costs if the funder withdraws, and whether the funder's obligation survives its exit, as the reported $350,000 arrangement suggests it can. Ask how much time remains on any limitation period and what happens to it if the case ends. And ask whether the case could realistically find a second funder, because in all three matters the answer appeared to be no. None of this is legal advice, and a lawyer who knows the jurisdiction should answer these questions for your own matter.
sources: Buttgieg v Macquarie Bank Limited [2026] FCA 1500, Federal Court of Australia (reasons published 9 October 2026)
Inger v State of Queensland [2026] FCA 792, Federal Court of Australia (22 June 2026)
ABC News, Queensland child safety racial discrimination class actions being discontinued in Federal Court (8 October 2026)
National Indigenous Times, Queensland First Nations child removals class action discontinued due to loss of funding (16 October 2026)
